newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra says native title settlement close.
newsitem.headline: Canberra says native title settlement close.

text.p: The Australian government said on Monday it was close to a settlement in the country's latest dispute over native title, which has pitched farmers against Aborigines and their newly gained rights to use rural land.

The rural-based National Party, a partner in the ruling Liberal-National coalition and always hostile to any loss of farmers' rights, endorsed the plan that Prime Minister John Howard has not yet announced.
"We are very close to finding a strong and unified approach to it," Deputy National Party Leader and Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said on radio.
The National Party has demanded that parliament simply extinguish the High Court's invention of native rights to pastoralists leases and compensate Aborigines for the loss.
But Anderson did not repeat that demand on Monday.

"There is a view being put that there are some manipulations around the edges of the actual approach taken which can still guarantee the sort of security that we have been seeking," he said when asked whether his party would accept anything less than extinguishment," he said.
"It may be that is possible ...," he said. "But our position is clear, our objectives are clear ...", Anderson said.
"We have to have the restoration of the certainty that we're looking for," he said.

Farmers -- and to a lesser extent miners -- have complained that uncertainty has crippled primary industries since the court in December unexpectedly ruled that Aborigines had unspecified rights to land that the government had let to pastoralists.

Prime Minister John Howard has been negotiating with both sides since the ruling but has said that if farmers and Aborigines cannot agree then he will impose a solution. He discussed one with Cabinet last week.
Newspapers reported on Monday that a key element of the plan would be to abolish any native title rights that were inconsistent with farmers carrying on pastoral activities.
But the plan would also guarantee access rights to the land for Aborigines.
The High Court originally invented native title in 1992, overturning the old assumption that Aborigines had owned nothing when the British settlers arrived on the continent in 1788.

The ruling, in the Mabo case, set of a prolonged and bitter dispute in which the former Labor government looked for a way of regulating native title and limiting any economic damage from it without discriminating against Aborigines.
But that settlement assumed that the court would not also impose native land rights on pastoral leases -- so the December Wik ruling has opened up the dispute again.
On Friday some Aboriginal leaders threatened to seek international trade sanctions against Australia over its handling of native title.
